title: Genetic Disorders, Part B

scenes.heading: Where we left off
scenes.body: Quick recap from Part A. Genetic disorders come in three kinds. Non-disjunction changes chromosome number. Single genes follow dominant and recessive patterns. Biotechnology diagnoses them, and screening flags risk while diagnosis confirms.

bullets.text: Three categories: single-gene, chromosomal, and multifactorial.
Single-gene disorders follow dominant, recessive or X-linked inheritance.
Protein and DNA tests diagnose them; screening flags risk, diagnosis confirms.

scenes.callout: Now we work a real pedigree.
scenes.caption: Quick recap of Part A before we continue.

voiceover.text: Welcome back. Quick recap from Part A. Genetic disorders fall into three kinds, and non disjunction is what changes chromosome number when cells divide. Single gene disorders follow dominant, recessive and X linked patterns that you can trace through a family. And biotechnology diagnoses them, with protein tests and DNA tests, where screening flags risk and a diagnostic test confirms. Right, with the inheritance rules fresh, let's work through a real pedigree question, and then see how two gene therapies actually work.

scenes.heading: What's the chance she's a carrier?
scenes.question: Both of Priya's parents are unaffected carriers of cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disease. Priya herself is unaffected. What is the probability that Priya is a carrier?
scenes.coachNote: List the genotypes from the cross, then condition on the fact that she is unaffected.
steps: Each parent is a carrier, written Aa, so the cross is Aa × Aa.
The offspring ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, where aa is affected.
Priya is unaffected, so she cannot be aa; that leaves only AA and Aa, in a 1 to 2 ratio.
Of those three unaffected outcomes, two are carriers (Aa), so the chance is 2 out of 3.
Answer: there is a 2/3, about 67%, probability that Priya is a carrier ✓
scenes.caption: Given she is unaffected, Priya has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier (1 AA : 2 Aa among unaffected).

voiceover.text: Let's do a genetics calculation, because conditional probability trips students up every year. Both of Priya's parents are unaffected carriers of cystic fibrosis, which is autosomal recessive. Priya herself is unaffected. What's the probability she's a carrier? Step one, write the cross. Each carrier parent is big A little a, so the cross is big A little a, times big A little a. Step two, the standard offspring ratio. That cross gives one big A big A, to two big A little a, to one little a little a, where little a little a would be affected. Step three, and this is the crucial move, we're told Priya is unaffected. So she cannot be little a little a. That removes the affected quarter entirely, leaving only the unaffected outcomes, one big A big A and two big A little a. Step four, count the carriers among what's left. Of those three unaffected possibilities, two are carriers, the big A little a ones. So the probability is two out of three, about sixty seven percent. The trick was conditioning on the information that she's unaffected, not just reading twenty five or fifty percent straight off the square.

scenes.heading: Gene therapy: three choices
scenes.body: Every gene therapy can be described by three choices: which cells, where the change happens, and what is done to the gene.

bullets.text: Somatic or germline: approved therapies change body cells only, so they are not inherited.
In vivo or ex vivo: inside the body, or on cells removed, changed and returned.
Add or edit: deliver a working copy with a viral vector, or edit DNA with CRISPR.

scenes.secondary: A viral vector is a virus with its disease-causing genes removed, used to carry a working gene into cells.
scenes.callout: Somatic, in vivo or ex vivo, add or edit: use these words to describe any gene therapy.
scenes.caption: Describe a gene therapy by cells (somatic), location (in vivo or ex vivo) and method (add or edit).

voiceover.text: Now, can we fix the gene itself? That's gene therapy, and any gene therapy can be described by three choices. First, which cells. Somatic gene therapy changes only body cells, so it isn't inherited, while germline therapy would change eggs, sperm or embryos, so it would be. Every approved gene therapy is somatic. Second, where the change happens. In vivo means inside the body, delivering the therapy straight to the tissue, while ex vivo means removing cells, changing them in the lab, and returning them. Third, what's done to the gene. You can add a working copy, usually carried by a viral vector, a virus with its disease causing genes removed. Or you can edit the existing DNA with a tool like CRISPR. Keep those three pairs in mind, because they're exactly how you outline the method of a gene therapy.

scenes.recapSeed: Gene therapies: somatic, in vivo or ex vivo, add or edit.

scenes.heading: Gene therapy 1: Luxturna for inherited blindness
scenes.body: Luxturna treats inherited retinal dystrophy, including some Leber congenital amaurosis, caused by two faulty RPE65 genes.

bullets.text: Cause: without RPE65, retinal cells cannot recycle the light-sensitive molecule, so vision fails.
Method: an AAV vector carrying working RPE65 is injected under the retina of each eye.
Outcome: treated patients navigated an obstacle course in much dimmer light; controls did not improve.

scenes.secondary: This is somatic, in vivo gene addition. It improves vision but does not restore normal sight, and it only works while enough retinal cells survive.
scenes.callout: Somatic, in vivo, adds a gene.

nodes.label: DNA test finds two faulty RPE65

scenes.caption: Luxturna: an AAV vector adds working RPE65 to retinal cells, improving vision in dim light.

voiceover.text: The first gene therapy is Luxturna, for an inherited retinal dystrophy that includes some cases of Leber congenital amaurosis. It's caused by two faulty copies of a gene called R P E sixty five. Without that enzyme, cells at the back of the retina can't recycle the light sensitive molecule the eye needs, so vision fades, often from childhood. Here's the method. First, a DNA test has to confirm two faulty R P E sixty five genes, which links straight back to diagnosis in Part A. Then, in surgery, a harmless adeno associated virus carrying a working R P E sixty five gene is injected under the retina of each eye. The retinal cells take up the gene and start making the enzyme. And the outcome, in the main trial, treated patients could find their way through an obstacle course in much dimmer light than before, while the untreated control group didn't improve. It doesn't give normal sight, but it's a real gain. So Luxturna is somatic, in vivo, and adds a gene.

scenes.heading: Gene therapy 2: Casgevy for sickle cell disease
scenes.body: Casgevy edits a patient's own blood stem cells outside the body so their red blood cells make fetal haemoglobin again.

bullets.text: Cause: a base substitution in the beta globin gene makes red blood cells sickle.
Method: stem cells are removed, CRISPR disables the BCL11A switch, and cells are returned after chemotherapy.
Outcome: in trials, over 90% of patients had no severe pain crises for at least a year.

scenes.secondary: Fetal haemoglobin does not sickle, so switching it back on reduces sickling. The chemotherapy needed to clear the bone marrow carries serious risks, including infertility.
scenes.callout: Somatic, ex vivo, edits a gene.
scenes.caption: Casgevy: ex vivo CRISPR editing of blood stem cells restores fetal haemoglobin and prevents crises.

voiceover.text: The second is Casgevy, for sickle cell disease, and it works in almost the opposite way. Sickle cell is caused by a base substitution in the beta globin gene, which makes red blood cells bend into a sickle shape, block small blood vessels, and cause severe pain crises. Here's the method. Doctors collect the patient's blood stem cells, and in the lab they use CRISPR to disable a genetic switch called B C L eleven A, which normally turns off fetal haemoglobin after birth. The patient then has strong chemotherapy to clear the bone marrow, and the edited cells are infused back. Their red blood cells now make fetal haemoglobin, which doesn't sickle. The outcome, in the trials, more than ninety percent of patients had no severe pain crises for at least a year. So Casgevy is somatic, ex vivo, and edits a gene. That contrast with Luxturna is exactly what a compare question wants.

scenes.heading: Ethical and legal implications
scenes.body: Gene therapies raise questions about access, consent and risk, and they are tightly regulated.

bullets.text: Access and equity: these one-off treatments cost from about US$850,000 to over US$2 million.
Consent and risk: patients, often children, must weigh unknown long-term effects.
Law in Australia: the TGA approves gene therapies and the Gene Technology Regulator licenses work with GMOs.
Heritable changes to the human genome are illegal in Australia.

scenes.secondary: Somatic therapy changes one patient. Germline editing would change every descendant, who cannot consent, which is why the law draws the line there.
scenes.callout: Who can access it, who consents, and where the law draws the line.
scenes.caption: Gene therapy raises cost, consent and risk issues; in Australia heritable human genome editing is illegal.

voiceover.text: Now the ethical and legal side, which the exam asks you to assess. Start with access and equity. These are one off treatments, but Luxturna costs about eight hundred and fifty thousand US dollars for both eyes, and Casgevy over two million. So who pays, and who misses out, especially since sickle cell disease is most common in lower income countries? Next, consent and risk. Many patients are children, so parents decide for them, and nobody yet knows the effects over a whole lifetime. Casgevy's chemotherapy, for example, can cause infertility. Then the law. In Australia, the Therapeutic Goods Administration has to approve a gene therapy before it can be used, and the Gene Technology Regulator licenses work with genetically modified organisms, which includes viral vectors. And making heritable changes to the human genome is illegal here, because a germline change would affect every descendant, none of whom can consent.

scenes.heading: Three traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: claiming CRISPR can now cure any genetic disease. Approved gene therapies cover only a handful of conditions, and delivery, off-target edits and cost still limit them.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: assuming chromosomal abnormalities are always inherited. Most trisomies are de novo, arising from non-disjunction in a parent with a normal karyotype. Trap 3: thinking gene therapy is passed to the patient's children. Approved therapies are somatic, so a treated parent can still pass on the faulty allele.
scenes.callout: Not a cure-all, often de novo, and somatic changes are not inherited.
scenes.caption: Gene therapy is not a cure-all; most trisomies are de novo; somatic therapy is not inherited.

voiceover.text: Three traps that quietly cost marks. Trap one, claiming CRISPR can now cure any genetic disease. It can't. Approved gene therapies cover only a handful of conditions, and getting the therapy into the right cells, avoiding off target edits, and the enormous cost all remain major barriers. Trap two, assuming chromosomal abnormalities are always inherited from a parent. Most trisomies, like trisomy twenty one, are de novo, arising from non disjunction in a parent's gametes, while the parent's own karyotype is completely normal. Trap three, thinking gene therapy fixes the problem for the patient's children too. Approved therapies are somatic, so a person successfully treated with Casgevy still carries the faulty allele in their eggs or sperm, and can still pass it on. Not a cure all, often de novo, and somatic means not inherited.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A mother is an unaffected carrier of haemophilia A, an X-linked recessive disorder. The father is unaffected. What is the probability that (a) a son is affected, and (b) a daughter is a carrier?
answerSteps: The mother is XᴴXʰ (carrier); the father is XᴴY (unaffected).
The four equally likely offspring are XᴴXᴴ, XᴴXʰ, XᴴY and XʰY.
(a) Sons are XᴴY or XʰY, and one of those two is affected, so the chance a son is affected is 1/2.
(b) Daughters are XᴴXᴴ or XᴴXʰ, and one of those two is a carrier, so the chance a daughter is a carrier is 1/2.
Answer: (a) a son is affected with probability 1/2, (b) a daughter is a carrier with probability 1/2 ✓
scenes.caption: Carrier mother × unaffected father: sons affected 1/2, daughters carriers 1/2.

voiceover.text: Quick check, an X linked cross. A mother is an unaffected carrier of haemophilia A, which is X linked recessive. The father is unaffected. What's the probability that, a, a son is affected, and b, a daughter is a carrier? Pause and draw the cross. Right, let's set it up. The mother has one normal and one faulty X, so she's big X H, big X little h. The father is unaffected, so he's big X H, Y. The four equally likely children are big X H big X H, big X H big X little h, big X H Y, and big X little h Y. Part a, the sons. A son gets the father's Y and one of the mother's X chromosomes, so he's either big X H Y, unaffected, or big X little h Y, affected. That's one in two. Part b, the daughters. A daughter gets the father's big X H plus one of the mother's X chromosomes, so she's either completely normal, or big X H big X little h, a carrier. Again one in two.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Condition on the information given: an unaffected child of two carriers is a carrier with probability 2/3.
Describe gene therapies as somatic or germline, in vivo or ex vivo, add or edit.
Luxturna: an AAV vector adds working RPE65 under the retina, improving vision in dim light.
Casgevy: blood stem cells edited ex vivo with CRISPR restore fetal haemoglobin, preventing pain crises.
Ethics and law: cost, consent and long-term risk; heritable human editing is illegal in Australia.
scenes.finalPrompt: Gene therapy question? Name it, then say somatic, in vivo or ex vivo, add or edit, and the outcome.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: conditional probability, the three choices, Luxturna, Casgevy, ethics and law.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five things to take away. First, in genetics problems, condition on the information you're given, so an unaffected child of two carriers is a carrier with a probability of two thirds. Second, describe any gene therapy with three pairs of words, somatic or germline, in vivo or ex vivo, add or edit. Third, Luxturna uses a viral vector to add a working R P E sixty five gene under the retina, improving vision in dim light. Fourth, Casgevy edits blood stem cells outside the body with CRISPR, so they make fetal haemoglobin and pain crises largely stop. And fifth, the ethics and law, cost and access, consent and long term risk, and in Australia heritable human genome editing is illegal. Whenever you meet a gene therapy, name it, classify it, and give its outcome. See you next lesson.
